frontmatter.title: FireIgnition: custom DEFAIR readers, lightning and new fires
frontmatter.subtitle: A Destination Earth / DEFAIR use case: three new readers for LSA SAF and H SAF products, and a study of lightning ignition over the Iberian Peninsula from an AI ready cube

children.value:
Every summer, some of the fires in the Iberian Peninsula are started by lightning. Two instruments on
the same Meteosat Third Generation satellite now see both sides of that story: the Lightning Imager
records every flash, and the Flexible Combined Imager detects the fires that appear afterwards. This
notebook brings them together with three more pieces of the picture: how dry the vegetation was, how
much rain fell with the storm, and how much water the air held before it. DEFAIR turns these six
products from four different sources into one AI ready data cube. The cube is then used to answer two
questions: is lightning followed by more new fires, and does dry weather make that effect stronger.
The notebook has two main sections:

Readers. Three of the six products have no built-in reader in DEFAIR. The process of writing and register a reader is explained step by step in detail using the reader of the Fire Risk Map, to be used like a native built-in reader. The other two readers follow the same process.

Analysis. The finished cube is opened from the project bucket with one call and used to answer two
research questions.
The cube is built in the companion notebook

. It reads
the raw products with the readers shown here, puts them on one regular grid, defines the case study settings and data preparation, defines the  fire label and saves the
result (cube) in the project’s bucket. You do not need to run it before this notebook!, it works only as support of the process and transparency.
In the Mediterranean Basin, lightning causes about 5 % of forest fires (

).
Lightning fires often start in remote areas, where they can spread before anyone detects and suppresses
them, and some become the largest fires of the summer. Dry thunderstorms, which bring lightning with little
rain, are considered an important cause of these fires (

). The question here is under which conditions a
lightning strike leads to a fire.
This analysis builds on earlier studies of lightning ignition in the Iberian Peninsula.

combined lightning, vegetation,
topography and weather data with logistic regression and random forests over central Spain.

used more than 17 million lightning strikes to train
a machine learning model of the daily probability of lightning ignition across the peninsula, from fuel,
vegetation and lightning characteristics.

examined the role of rain during thunderstorms. The delay between the strike and the detection of the fire
is called the holdover time (window), and it is usually short: in the Swiss Alps, most fires were detected within 24
hours of the igniting strike (
give a global overview of holdover times.

This use case applies the same approach with a new observing system. The MTG Lightning Imager is the first
geostationary optical lightning detector over Europe (

The Flexible Combined Imager on the same satellite detects fires every ten minutes, so lightning and fires
are observed from one platform on the same time scale. Fire data from space are consistent across national
borders and do not depend on national records of fire causes. Satellite products also describe the air
before the storm and the rain during it, both important for the dry thunderstorms behind large fires
(

All inputs are available operationally and come from EUMETSAT and its Satellite Application Facilities, so
the same analysis can be repeated for each new fire season.

The study covers the 37 convective episodes between 1 July and 9 September 2026 over the Iberian Peninsula,
on wildland cover used as mask for the aoi: needle-leaved trees, broadleaved deciduous and evergreen trees, shrubs and permanent
herbaceous vegetation.
RQ1. Do wildland cells hit by lightning have a

probability of a new fire in the 48 hours after the
first flash than the same cells without lightning under similar rain?
RQ2. Does that excess risk depend on how dry the fuel is and how much water the air held before the storm?

RQ2 compares that relative risk between dry and wet conditions. If dry thunderstorms are the ones that start
fires, the relative risk should be larger where the fuel is drier and where the air held less water:
RR(dry) > RR(wet). RQ2 is exploratory: it measures the size and direction of the effect, does dryness change what a flash does?.
Here a logistic regression and XGboost algorithms are used to answer the second question.

The raw products were copied once into the project bucket, unchanged except for two of them: the LSA-509 full
disc files were cut to a fixed Iberian window of rows and columns, and CLC+ was aggregated to the vegetation classes
and resampled to 10km cell

An episode, or storm day, is one calendar (July-September) day of the 2026 season  (00:00 to 24:00 UTC) with significant
lightning over the study area. To screen the season cheaply, only three of the 144 daily flash files were
read for each day, at 13:00, 17:00 and 21:00 UTC (highest convective time in a summer day),

and the day was kept when they held at least (>=100) flashes
over Iberia
. A short storm that fell entirely between those slots can be missed. The season scan found 37 episodes.
The companion notebook shows in detail how each of these is built.

One sample is one 10 km cell on one storm day. A cell is exposed when the Lightning Imager saw at least one
flash in it that day. The instrument counts all lightning and cannot tell the flashes that reach the ground
from those that stay in the cloud.

Each flash is moved back along the satellite’s line of sight to a cloud height of 10 km. Without this
correction a flash over Iberia appears about one cell too far north
(

Each cell has its own 48 hour window. It starts at the first flash in the cell, or at the storm time of the
day when no flash fell there. A fire first seen inside the window counts as new.

A cell is left out of a storm day when it, or one of its eight neighbours, already had a fire in the 48
hours before the window, or when the satellite could see fires in less than a quarter of its window.

Pixels with detections in three periods a week apart, or on twenty or more days, are treated as fixed heat
sources such as gas flares, and removed together with their eight neighbours.
Each fire is counted once. A fire inside the windows of two storm days goes to the most recent storm.

A cell with lightning is compared with the same cell on other days without lightning and with similar rain,
which keeps its terrain, vegetation and human activity fixed.(groups of cell with same conditions are compared)

) only exist under clear sky, so they are read between three hours and one hour
before the storm time.
There is no record of what lit each fire, so the study measures association, not causation.

DEFAIR does not open product files directly. It uses a reader: a small plugin that knows the structure of
one file format and turns its contents into an
A reader is a Python class that inherits from
. The base class handles the underlying file access, including opening the

, regardless of its storage location or source. The file may reside on a local disk, in an S3 bucket, or in the HDA. This abstraction means readers do not need to manage credentials, storage protocols, or file downloads. The same reader implementation can process files from any supported source without changes.
Once a product has a reader, DEFAIR handles it like any other supported product. It can:
stream the data directly from S3,
read many files in one call,
crop, reproject and align it with other sources.

The product could also be converted outside DEFAIR and imported as plain arrays, but then none of these
operations would be available. DEFAIR ships built-in readers for the METOP, MTG, Sentinel-3, MSG native and
ERA5 families, among others. For any other product you can write your own reader and register it as a
plugin, and DEFAIR then treats it exactly like a built-in one.

The pixels still have no position on Earth. The Fire Risk Map is not the full disc of the satellite but a
window over Europe and North Africa. The file’s metadata says where that window sits, following the
navigation standard of the Coordination Group for Meteorological Satellites (CGMS): the attributes

are the column and the row of the window where the centre of the disc falls. The centre of the full
disc is always the same pixel, so the row and column where the window starts follow by subtraction. Both
numbers come from the header of the file.

, is

in CF form, so any tool can compute the latitude and

must frame the Iberian Peninsula.

# H SAF H61B daily precipitation: the same four steps, written as one class.
# H61B covers the same SEVIRI full disc as the Fire Risk Map, so it reuses DISK_SIZE, DISK_EXTENT and GEOS_ATTRS from step 3.
class HSAFH61Reader(DataReaderPlugin):
    PRIORITY = 60
    FILENAME_PATTERN = re.compile(r"h61_(\d{8})_0000_24_fdk\.nc\.gz$")

    @classmethod
    def can_handle(cls, path):
        return bool(cls.FILENAME_PATTERN.search(str(path)))

    def read(self, path, source=None, source_kwargs=None):
        # 1. Open: the file is gzipped NetCDF, so it is decompressed in memory first
        sealed = pd.to_datetime(self.FILENAME_PATTERN.search(str(path)).group(1))
        with self.open_file(path, source, source_kwargs) as f:
            raw = gzip.decompress(f.read())
        engine = "h5netcdf" if raw[:4] == b"\x89HDF" else "scipy"
        ds = xr.open_dataset(io.BytesIO(raw), engine=engine)[["acc_rr"]].load()

        # 2. Physical values: acc_rr is already in mm, so only the dimensions need their usual names
        ds = ds.rename(dict(zip(ds.acc_rr.dims, ("y", "x"))))

        # 3. Georeference: the file is the full disc, so every pixel centre follows from the disc extent
        dx = (DISK_EXTENT[2] - DISK_EXTENT[0]) / DISK_SIZE
        centres = np.arange(DISK_SIZE) + 0.5
        ds = ds.assign_coords(
            x=("x", DISK_EXTENT[0] + centres * dx, {"standard_name": "projection_x_coordinate", "units": "m", "axis": "X"}),
            y=("y", DISK_EXTENT[3] - centres * dx, {"standard_name": "projection_y_coordinate", "units": "m", "axis": "Y"}),
        )
        ds["acc_rr"].attrs["grid_mapping"] = "geostationary"

        # 4. Time and metadata: the file sealed on day D+1 at 00:00 holds the rain of day D
        ds = ds.expand_dims(time=[sealed - pd.Timedelta(days=1)])
        ds = ds.assign_coords(geostationary=xr.DataArray(np.int32(0), attrs=GEOS_ATTRS))
        ds.attrs = {"Conventions": "CF-1.8", "source": "H SAF H61B daily accumulated precipitation, MSG SEVIRI full disc"}
        return Dataset(ds.chunk(), cdm=self._build_cdm())

    @staticmethod
    def _build_cdm():
        # A grid on a geostationary projection, so DEFAIR can reproject it onto any target grid
        grid = GriddedModel(id="hsaf_h61_grid", variables=("acc_rr",), crs="GEOS", dims=("y", "x"),
                            x_dim="x", y_dim="y", x_coord="x", y_coord="y", grid_mapping="geostationary",
                            geostationary=GeostationaryParams(satellite_longitude=0.0, perspective_point_height=35785831.0,
                                                              sweep_axis="y", grid_mapping="geostationary"))
        return CommonDataModel(reader="hsaf_h61", product_family="hsaf", spatial_groups=(grid,), temporal_groups=())

# LSA SAF FRP-Pixel (LSA-509): one file holds two products with different shapes, so the reader returns one
# of them, chosen with `product`: "fires", a list of fire detections (points), or "quality", an image that
# says where fire detection was possible (a grid on the MTG geostationary projection).
FCI_CENTRE, FCI_STEP = 5567.5, 1000.0                  # centre and pixel size of the 1 km FCI disc [pixels, m]
MTG_GEOS_ATTRS = {
    "grid_mapping_name": "geostationary",
    "longitude_of_projection_origin": 0.0,
    "latitude_of_projection_origin": 0.0,
    "perspective_point_height": 35786400.0,
    "sweep_angle_axis": "y",
    "semi_major_axis": 6378137.0,
    "semi_minor_axis": 6356752.31414,
    "false_easting": 0.0,
    "false_northing": 0.0,
}

class LSA509FRPReader(DataReaderPlugin):
    PRIORITY = 60
    FILENAME_PATTERN = re.compile(r"LSA509_iberia_(\d{8})\.nc$")

    @classmethod
    def can_handle(cls, path):
        return bool(cls.FILENAME_PATTERN.search(str(path)))

    def read(self, path, source=None, source_kwargs=None, product="fires"):
        f = self.open_file(path, source, source_kwargs)
        if product == "fires":
            date = int(self.FILENAME_PATTERN.search(str(path)).group(1))
            return self._read_fires(f, date)
        return self._read_quality(f)

    @staticmethod
    def _read_fires(f, date):
        # Points: one row per fire, with a unique id per day and the parallax corrected position as coordinates
        ds = xr.open_dataset(f, engine="h5netcdf", group="ListProduct", chunks={})
        ds = ds.assign_coords(fire=date * 100_000 + ds.fire.values)
        ds = ds.set_coords(["LATITUDE_PARALLAX", "LONGITUDE_PARALLAX", "LATITUDE", "LONGITUDE", "ACQTIME"])
        ds["LATITUDE_PARALLAX"].attrs.update(standard_name="latitude", units="degrees_north")
        ds["LONGITUDE_PARALLAX"].attrs.update(standard_name="longitude", units="degrees_east")
        ds["LATITUDE"].attrs.pop("standard_name", None)
        ds["LONGITUDE"].attrs.pop("standard_name", None)
        # build_point_cdm declares point data: DEFAIR then knows it cannot be resampled like a grid
        cdm = build_point_cdm(reader="lsa509_frp", product_family="lsa_saf", ds=ds, sample_dim="fire",
                              latitude="LATITUDE_PARALLAX", longitude="LONGITUDE_PARALLAX", time_coord="ACQTIME",
                              time_representation="per_sample_observation")
        return Dataset(ds, cdm=cdm)

    @staticmethod
    def _read_quality(f):
        # Grid: rows and columns of the FCI disc become projection coordinates in metres
        ds = xr.open_dataset(f, engine="h5netcdf", group="QualityProduct", chunks={"time": 1}, mask_and_scale=False)
        ds = ds.assign_coords(
            x=("samp", (ds.samp.values - FCI_CENTRE) * FCI_STEP, {"standard_name": "projection_x_coordinate", "units": "m", "axis": "X"}),
            y=("line", (FCI_CENTRE - ds.line.values) * FCI_STEP, {"standard_name": "projection_y_coordinate", "units": "m", "axis": "Y"}),
        ).swap_dims(samp="x", line="y")
        ds["qualityflag"].attrs["grid_mapping"] = "geostationary"
        ds["geostationary"] = xr.DataArray(np.int32(0), attrs=MTG_GEOS_ATTRS)
        grid = GriddedModel(id="lsa509_quality_grid", variables=("qualityflag",), crs="GEOS", dims=("y", "x"),
                            x_dim="x", y_dim="y", x_coord="x", y_coord="y", grid_mapping="geostationary",
                            geostationary=GeostationaryParams(satellite_longitude=0.0, perspective_point_height=35786400.0,
                                                              sweep_axis="y", grid_mapping="geostationary"))
        cdm = CommonDataModel(reader="lsa509_frp", product_family="lsa_saf", spatial_groups=(grid,), temporal_groups=())
        return Dataset(ds, cdm=cdm)

children.value: The relative risk compares cells with and without lightning on the same storm day. It is the share of cells with lightning that had a new fire, divided by the share of cells without lightning that had one. A value of 1 means lightning makes no difference, and a value above 1 means cells hit by lightning burn more often.

A cell hit by lightning should be compared with a cell that is similar in every other way. The Mantel-Haenszel estimator (Mantel and Haenszel, 1959) does this by splitting the data into small groups, called strata. It computes the comparison inside each stratum and then combines them, giving more weight to the larger ones. Here each stratum is one cell under one rain class, so a cell with lightning is compared only with the same cell on days with similar rain and no lightning. A stratum counts only if it has days with lightning, days without lightning and at least one fire; the cell below reports how many do. For contrast, it also prints the crude relative risk, computed without strata.

Cells on the same day share the same storm and weather, so they are not independent of each other. The uncertainty is therefore estimated by resampling whole storm days. The 37 days are drawn at random with replacement, 1000 times, and the relative risk is recomputed each time. This is called a cluster bootstrap. The 95 % interval covers the middle 95 % of the 1000 values.

A fire can fall inside the windows of two storm days. The main rule assigns it to the storm day whose window started last. The last two lines of output repeat the estimate with two other rules. The first gives the fire to the last storm day with lightning in the cell, which can only raise the estimate. The second leaves out every fire shared by a day with lightning and a day without, which lowers it, because it also drops fires that lightning started on consecutive storm days. The main rule gives a value between the two.

def strata(df):
    """Fires and cells with and without lightning in every stratum of the study design."""
    return (df.assign(n1=df.exposed, n0=1 - df.exposed, a=df.fire_new * df.exposed, c=df.fire_new * (1 - df.exposed))
              .groupby(STRATA, observed=True)[["a", "c", "n1", "n0"]].sum())

def mantel_haenszel_rr(df):
    """Relative risk of the exposed cells, pooled over the strata of the study design."""
    s = strata(df)
    n = s.n1 + s.n0
    denominator = (s.c * s.n1 / n).sum()
    return (s.a * s.n0 / n).sum() / denominator if denominator > 0 else np.nan   # nan: no fire without lightning

def episode_bootstrap(df, stat, n):
    """The statistic recomputed on n resamples of whole episodes, drawn with replacement."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    parts = [g for _, g in df.groupby("episode")]
    return np.array([stat(pd.concat([parts[i] for i in rng.integers(0, len(parts), len(parts))])) for _ in range(n)])

def with_interval(df, stat, n):
    """The statistic and its 95 % interval from n resamples of whole episodes."""
    low, high = np.nanpercentile(episode_bootstrap(df, stat, n), [2.5, 97.5], axis=0)
    return stat(df), low, high

def repeated_fires(cube, sample, prefer_exposed=False, drop_mixed=False):
    """True where the fire of the cell is left out because it falls in the windows of several episodes.
    It is kept in the episode whose window started last; with prefer_exposed, in the last episode with
    lightning in the cell; with drop_mixed, a fire shared by episodes with and without lightning in the
    cell is left out of all of them. The cube was built with the first rule."""
    t = (xr.Dataset({"fire_first": cube.fire_first.where(sample), "start": cube.label_start, "exposed": cube.exposed})
         .to_dataframe().dropna(subset=["fire_first"]).reset_index())
    t["key"] = t.start + (1e10 * t.exposed if prefer_exposed else 0)
    owner = t.loc[t.groupby(["y", "x", "fire_first"]).key.idxmax(), ["y", "x", "fire_first", "episode"]]
    dup = t.merge(owner.rename(columns={"episode": "owner"}), on=["y", "x", "fire_first"]).query("episode != owner")
    if drop_mixed:
        mixed = t.groupby(["y", "x", "fire_first"]).exposed.transform("nunique") > 1
        dup = pd.concat([dup, t[mixed]])

    mask = np.zeros(cube.fire_new.shape, bool)
    mask[pd.Index(cube.episode.values).get_indexer(dup.episode),
         pd.Index(cube.y.values).get_indexer(dup.y),
         pd.Index(cube.x.values).get_indexer(dup.x)] = True
    return xr.DataArray(mask, coords=cube.fire_new.coords, dims=cube.fire_new.dims)

def plot_intervals(ax, estimate, low, high, labels, horizontal=False):
    """Estimates with their 95 % intervals, and a dashed line at 1, the value of no effect."""
    pos, err = np.arange(len(estimate)), [np.asarray(estimate - low), np.asarray(high - estimate)]
    if horizontal:
        ax.errorbar(estimate, pos, xerr=err, fmt="o", color="k")
        ax.axvline(1, ls="--", color="grey")
        ax.set_yticks(pos, labels)
    else:
        ax.errorbar(pos, estimate, yerr=err, fmt="o", color="k")
        ax.axhline(1, ls="--", color="grey")
        ax.set_xticks(pos, labels)

Probably yes, but one season is not enough to be sure. Cells hit by lightning had more new fires than the same
cells on days with similar rain and no lightning, but the 95 % interval still includes 1, so H0 cannot be
rejected.

The answer stays open because lightning lights only a small share of the fires, and the label counts new fires
of every cause. In one season that leaves about a hundred fires in cells with lightning, and the effect of the
flashes is mixed with many fires that would have happened anyway.

The checks point the same way, which makes the effect likely to be real. When the lightning is shuffled
between days, the relative risk falls back to about 1 and rarely reaches the real value. Fires in cells with
lightning appear sooner after the flash, which is what an ignition by lightning looks like. More flashes bring
more fires, except in the cells with the most flashes, possibly because the strongest storms also bring the
most rain; with so few fires that last class cannot be read.

How fires that fall inside the windows of two storm days are counted matters. Giving them to the last storm
with lightning raises the estimate. Leaving out the ones shared by a day with and a day without lightning drops
it below 1, but that rule removes about half of the fires in cells with lightning, because lightning often
strikes the same area on consecutive days. The main rule, the most recent storm, can only err against
lightning, so the estimate is, if anything, on the low side.

Lightning is most likely to start a fire when it strikes
without rain, in what is known as a dry thunderstorm (Rorig and Ferguson, 1999). The difference
between a dry and a wet storm is decided before the storm begins, by how much water the air holds.

DRY STORM                                WET STORM

   dry air before the storm               moist air before the storm
   (little precipitable water)            (much precipitable water)

        .------------------.                   .------------------.
       (    storm cloud     )                 (    storm cloud     )
        '------------------'                   '------------------'
            \     :  :  :                          \     | | | |
            /     rain dries up                    /     | | | |
            \     on the way down                  \     | | | |

      lightning hits dry vegetation          lightning hits wet vegetation
      nothing puts the spark out             the rain puts the spark out

      a new fire is MORE likely              a new fire is LESS likely

In the Mediterranean, the storms that start fires tend to have a high cloud base, less water in the
air than usual and little rain (Pérez-Invernón et al., 2021). The GII measures that water in the air,
and how unstable the air is, in the hours before the storm. Rorig and Ferguson (1999) told dry from
wet storm days using the temperature difference between 850 and 500 hPa, the same difference the
K-index is built on.

If this idea holds, cells hit by lightning should burn more often when the air held less water, when
less rain fell and when the vegetation was drier. The rain itself is measured by H61B, but only as a
daily total, which cannot say whether it fell before, with or after the lightning. The GII fills part
of that gap by describing what kind of storm it was.

bootstrap interval, says how much dry weather changes the effect. The precipitable water only exists

children.value:
Two models look at the cells hit by lightning and try to tell the ones that burned from the ones that
did not. The outcome is a new fire in the window, of any cause. Ten features describe each cell: the
rain of the day; the three fuel moisture codes (

), without the Fire
Weather Index, which is built from them; the number of flashes, on a logarithmic scale, and their mean
duration; the tree cover; the day of the season and the north to south position of the cell, which take
care of seasonal and regional trends; and

, the new fire rate of the same cell on days
without lightning, which carries the background risk of the place. The GII is left out of the models,
because it only exists under clear sky and would remove many cells.

The main model is a logistic regression on standardised features, fitted without penalty so that
its effects are not shrunk. XGBoost, a gradient boosted tree model that can capture non linear
effects, is the contrast. Both are trained on the data as they are, without class weights, so their
outputs can be read as probabilities. Each model is trained on 36 storm days and tested on the one left
out, 37 times, so a day is never used for training and testing at once.

Two scores summarise the predictions. The AUC-PR measures how well a model ranks the cells that
burned above the others; a model without skill scores the prevalence, the share of cells with a fire.
The Brier score is the mean squared error of the predicted probabilities; lower is better. Accuracy
is not used: with fewer than one cell in a hundred burning, a model that always says “no fire” is almost
always right and has learned nothing.

Finally, the logistic regression is fitted on all the storm days to estimate its odds ratios, with 95 %
intervals from the same cluster bootstrap. An odds ratio above 1 means the chance of a new fire rises
with the feature, below 1 that it falls, and an interval that crosses 1 means the data cannot tell the
direction. The three fuel codes describe the same system, so they share their effect and widen each
other’s intervals.

hit = table[table.exposed == 1].copy()
hit["cell_base_rate"] = hit.cell.map(table[table.exposed == 0].groupby("cell").fire_new.mean())
hit["lfl_flash_count"] = np.log1p(hit.lfl_flash_count)
complete = hit[FEATURES_RQ2].notna().all(axis=1)
print(f"cells hit by lightning: {len(hit)} | with every feature: {int(complete.sum())} | "
      f"new fires among them: {int(hit.fire_new[complete].sum())}")

hit = hit[complete]
X_rq2, y_rq2, groups_rq2 = hit[FEATURES_RQ2], hit.fire_new.astype(int), hit.episode

def logistic():
    return make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, max_iter=1000))

def boosted():
    return XGBClassifier(n_estimators=300, max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.05, subsample=0.8,
                         random_state=SEED)

oof = pd.DataFrame(index=hit.index, columns=["logistic", "xgboost"], dtype=float)
for train, test in LeaveOneGroupOut().split(X_rq2, y_rq2, groups_rq2):
    X_train, y_train = X_rq2.iloc[train], y_rq2.iloc[train]
    oof.iloc[test, 0] = logistic().fit(X_train, y_train).predict_proba(X_rq2.iloc[test])[:, 1]
    oof.iloc[test, 1] = boosted().fit(X_train, y_train).predict_proba(X_rq2.iloc[test])[:, 1]

prevalence = y_rq2.mean()
scores = pd.DataFrame({m: {"AUC-PR": average_precision_score(y_rq2, p), "Brier": brier_score_loss(y_rq2, p)}
                       for m, p in oof.items()}).T
scores.loc["no skill (prevalence)"] = [prevalence, prevalence * (1 - prevalence)]
display(scores.round(4))

# The effect of each condition, from the logistic regression fitted on all the storm days
coef_of = lambda df: logistic().fit(df[FEATURES_RQ2], df.fire_new.astype(int))[-1].coef_[0]
coef, ci_low, ci_high = with_interval(hit, coef_of, N_BOOT)
odds = pd.DataFrame({"odds ratio": np.exp(coef), "2.5 %": np.exp(ci_low), "97.5 %": np.exp(ci_high)}, index=FEATURES_RQ2)
display(odds.round(3))

o = odds.sort_values("odds ratio")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
plot_intervals(ax, o["odds ratio"], o["2.5 %"], o["97.5 %"], o.index, horizontal=True)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("odds ratio per standard deviation (95 % interval)")
ax.set_title("Logistic regression, cells hit by lightning")
plt.tight_layout()

Not in a way this season can show. Split into dry and wet thirds, the sample keeps only a handful to a few
dozen fires with lightning in each third. The relative risks of the thirds overlap, and the ratio between the
driest and the wettest third stays close to 1 with very wide intervals. The dry thunderstorm idea is not
contradicted; one season does not hold enough lightning fires to test it.

Neither model does clearly better than a model without skill, so the conditions of the day do not tell the
cells that burned from the others. The only two features with a clear effect are the day of the season and
the background fire rate of the cell. After lightning, a new fire is more likely late in the summer and in
places that burn often anyway; the properties of the storm itself make no visible difference.
The results hold within the limits of the data, gathered here in one place.
What it does to the results
Parallax corrected with one fixed height
Flashes from clouds much lower or higher than 10 km keep part of their shift, so a few land in a neighbouring cell. This pushes the relative risk towards 1
All lightning, not only ground strikes
Only flashes that reach the ground can light a fire, but the Lightning Imager also counts those inside the cloud. Exposure is broader than real contact with the ground
The label counts every new fire, whatever lit it. Lightning starts a small share of the fires, so its effect is measured on a small part of them
H61B is a daily total at about 3 km. It cannot tell whether the rain fell before or after a flash
The instability indices only exist under clear sky, and they are read before the storm over the whole study area, not before the first flash in each cell
The FCI sees a fire only above a minimum power and not under clouds. Small or smouldering fires are missed, and the time to detection is an upper bound of the holdover
Fixed sources from the same season
The rules that remove industrial sources are computed on the season they clean, with reasoned thresholds, and removing eight neighbours can remove a real fire next to a source
The Fire Risk Map is a 24 hour forecast and carries the error of the forecast weather
Three years before the season studied
All results come from 2026, which limits the number of fires and widens every interval

The notebook took six products from four providers to two answers. On the way it showed four things about
working with DEFAIR.

Readers can be added. Three products without a reader came in through three small plugins, registered with
a standard entry point and used exactly like the built-in readers.

Very different sources end on one grid. In the companion notebook, gridded and point products,
geostationary and projected, become layers of the same cells through the same read, crop, reproject and
align steps.
The cube is the handover. One

call is the whole link between the data preparation and the
analysis, and the same cube feeds a stratified statistical comparison and two machine learning models.

A cube that carries its context supports careful statistics. Every cell has its label, window, identity,
rain, visibility and storm day, so it can be compared with itself, the design can be checked against shuffled
lightning, models can be tested without mixing days, cells the satellite could not see stay out of the
sample, and each fire is counted once.

New fires were more frequent in cells hit by lightning than in the same cells without it, and the checks of the
design support that this is not chance, but one season leaves the result short of statistical proof (RQ1). Dry
fuel and dry air did not change the effect in a way the data can show, and the best signs of a fire after
lightning were the time of the summer and the place (RQ2).

Lightning starts about 15 % of the forest fires of the Mediterranean Basin
(

so the effect of lightning is measured on a small part of the fires. More seasons, which the same pipeline can
process, or records of fire causes would sharpen it. The results describe how often new fires followed
lightning in one season, not the cause of any single fire.
